title: Media Ownership
blurb: Concentration, regulation and the platforms: parliament on the press.

brief.question: What does the parliamentary record show about media ownership?
brief.answer:
The strongest and most decision-relevant finding in the record is that Labor speakers repeatedly argued that Australia already had a highly concentrated media market, dominated by Rupert Murdoch’s News Ltd and the Packer family’s Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd, and that the Howard government’s proposed changes would make concentration worse. Labor quoted figures showing News Ltd controlled two-thirds of capital city and national newspapers, almost three-quarters of Sunday newspapers, almost half of suburban newspapers and a quarter of regional newspapers, with a quarter share in Foxtel. PBL was said to reach more than half the potential television audience, publish 65 magazines, and hold major online and pay-TV interests. Against this, one Labor speaker cited research that 80 per cent of Australians opposed further media concentration, and another cited Productivity Commission findings that a proprietor’s business and editorial interests were likely to influence content and opinion. Cross-media rules introduced under the Keating government in the late 1980s were defended as preventing any one proprietor being both “queen of the screen” and “prince of print,” and as preserving at least some diversity.

The debate shifted over time through repeated attempts at legislative change: the Broadcasting Services Amendment (Media Ownership) Bill 2002, a second 2002 bill, and the 2006 bill. The government’s stated case, put by Senator Alston and others, was that ownership of media “per se is irrelevant,” that new media and the internet created a “plethora of sources,” and that separate editorial processes could protect diversity. Labor responded with evidence that most Australians still relied on traditional media—88 per cent used free-to-air television for news, 76 per cent used radio and 76 per cent used newspapers, while only 10 per cent used pay TV and 11 per cent used the internet—and that the major internet news sites were owned by the same established media players. Labor also noted that the 2002 bill initially would have allowed one proprietor to own television, newspapers and radio in one market, and that after Senate lobbying the government signalled it might settle for two of the three, which Labor said exposed the real agenda.

The sharpest disagreement was over whether ownership itself determines media content and democratic influence. Labor speakers insisted that “he who pays the piper calls the tune” and that no editorial separation test could protect the public when a proprietor can hire and fire journalists and set the ultimate direction. They rejected the idea that journalists’ independence could be separated from their employer’s commercial interests, and attacked Australian Broadcasting Authority chairman Professor David Flint for arguing ownership did not dominate content. Labor also accused the government of hypocrisy, noting that coalition backbenchers such as the member for Hinkler, the future Minister for Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs, and the Minister for Education, Science and Training had spoken strongly against concentration in the 1990s but were silent once on the front bench. The most incendiary charge came from the member for Lowe, who alleged a secret deal between Prime Minister Howard and Kerry Packer dating from 1995, called the 2006 bill a “disgraceful piece of chicanery,” and claimed it would allow PBL to use a war chest of between $4½ billion and $4¾ billion—or possibly $6 billion—to buy more casino assets and dominate media, including acquiring Fairfax.

On promises versus outcomes, the record shows the government promised safeguards, but Labor said those promises were hollow. In answer to a question from the member for Lowe, the Prime Minister said the bill would use exemptions and undertakings to maintain existing levels of locally produced news and current affairs and to require separate editorial processes. Labor dismissed this as nonsense, noting it said nothing about dominant city markets and would entrench concentration rather than protect diversity. Labor also argued that the proposed editorial separation test would create unprecedented government interference in media operations, a position criticised by the Australian Press Council and Fairfax as well as by public-interest and industry groups. Despite the government’s claims that its changes would enhance diversity, Labor concluded that the effect would be to create three huge conglomerates, allow Packer to buy Fairfax, and allow Murdoch to take a free-to-air network, leaving Australia with greater concentration, fewer independent newsrooms, and a diminished capacity for the media to hold governments accountable.

sections.question: What have MPs said about media ownership concentration in Australia?
sections.answer:
Australian parliamentarians have repeatedly warned that further media ownership concentration threatens democracy and the public interest. Labor MPs, including the member for Throsby, have argued that allowing proprietors to own television, radio, and newspapers in the same market would "attack our democracy at its very heart" and reduce diversity, competition, and consumer choice. They have cited Paul Keating's principle that media owners should be either "queens of the screen" or "princes of print," not both.

Government backbenchers have also voiced concerns. In 1995, the member for Hinkler warned of "the centralising of media control" and called for a stand against it. The member for Moreton (later Minister for Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs) said in 1996 that "diversity has all but disappeared" due to concentration, and in 2000 noted that cross-media rules were becoming redundant but owners should "exercise some real responsibility." The member for Bradfield (later Minister for Education, Science and Training) said in 1997 that his constituents would not support further concentration and that a proprietor controlling TV and newspapers in Sydney and Melbourne was "not a legacy we wish to leave upon our children." Critics have accused these frontbenchers of hypocrisy for abandoning those views once in government.

The Australian Greens have stated that Australia has "the most concentrated media ownership in the Western world" and that this is "corrosive of the fabric of Australian democracy." They have called for keeping the two-out-of-three rule as a minimum safeguard.

Specific figures cited include News Limited owning 147 newspapers, with daily and Sunday titles accounting for over 69% of total circulation, and metropolitan sales potentially reaching around 80% if Monday-to-Friday calculations are used. Kerry Stokes, proprietor of the Seven Network, admitted to a parliamentary committee that abolishing the 75% reach rule could let him "absolutely dominate" media in Western Australia, which he conceded was not in the public interest.

sections.question: What was said about the news media bargaining code and tech platforms?
sections.answer:
The news media bargaining code was repeatedly framed as a world-first Australian response to a stark bargaining power imbalance between global digital platforms—chiefly Google and Meta (Facebook)—and Australian news businesses. Speakers from the Coalition credited their government with initiating the reform in 2019 after voluntary negotiations failed, delivering the mandatory code in 2021. They claimed it produced more than 30 commercial agreements worth an estimated $250 million annually to Australian news organisations, citing deals with Seven West, Nine, Fairfax, and Junkee Media as evidence it worked. The Coalition stressed the code’s negotiate-arbitrate model, with the Treasurer designating platforms based on ACCC advice, and highlighted minimum standards like 14 days’ notice of algorithm changes and a default offer mechanism for smaller and regional publishers.

Labor acknowledged the code’s initial success but argued its design had a critical loophole: platforms could avoid obligations by removing news from their services, as Meta did briefly in Australia in 2021 and later in Canada. Labor noted Meta’s April 2024 decision not to renew commercial agreements—estimated at around $70 million a year—and its threat to drop news entirely, giving a company with enormous market power a bargaining tool. Labor’s proposed fix was a "news bargaining incentive" scheme, a market-based model with a clear preference for commercial deals, but with a charge on non-compliant platforms, with every dollar returned to the sector to support journalists.

Other positions included concerns from a speaker who noted 106 local and regional newspapers closed between 2008 and 2018, nearly doubling to 200 since 2019, and worried the code might disadvantage smaller outlets while criticising the government’s undermining of workers’ collective bargaining rights. Independent Senator Rex Patrick’s amendments to address opaque algorithms and big tech business practices were defeated in the Senate on 24 February 2021 by a vote of 12 to 32. Labor also raised concerns about ministerial discretion, potential legal challenges, and a lack of mechanisms to ensure the code increased media diversity or journalist employment, while criticising the Morrison government for not addressing other ACCC recommendations and for lacking transparency on how platform payments were used.

sections.question: What has parliament said about the Screen and Digital Games Industries Bill 2025?
sections.answer:
The Screen and Digital Games Industries Bill 2025 was debated in the New South Wales Parliament, where it received cross-party support. The bill repeals the Film and Television Industry Act 1988 and replaces it with a new Screen and Digital Games Industries Act, modernising terminology to include the digital games industry. It also establishes a Screen and Digital Games Industries Advisory Committee, replacing the former Film and Television Industry Advisory Committee, and amends the Local Government Act 1993 to support a "screen production friendly" council accreditation scheme.

The Government, led by Minister John Graham, framed the bill as supporting jobs and growth, noting that New South Wales is home to 22 per cent of Australia's game studios and 16 per cent of its full-time games employees, despite 81 per cent of Australians playing games. The Government also highlighted measures accompanying the bill, including lowering the minimum expenditure threshold for rebates from $500,000 to $350,000 and investing $1.5 million over three years in digital games programs. The Opposition supported the bill but moved an amendment, moved by Kevin Anderson, to require that at least one advisory committee member have relevant industry experience and reside or work in regional New South Wales. The Government supported this amendment, and it was agreed to. The Greens also supported the bill, with Jenny Leong emphasising the need for diversity on the committee and for broader funding of creatives.

sections.question: What has parliament said about Liberal Party and media ownership?
sections.answer:
Several passages address the Liberal Party and media ownership, though none describe the party itself owning media. One speaker, identified only as a member of parliament, claims there is a "shady, dodgy network of right-wing think tanks, all associated with an international umbrella group of think tanks, the Atlas Network, all associated with the Liberal Party—and now they're buying our media assets." The same speaker says this is why investing in public interest journalism and a media "free of commercial and political interests" has never been more important.

Another passage, from a senator in the Commonwealth Parliament, alleges that "Senator Scarr" could see "another media outlet in this country that was claiming until recently that it was directly associated with ADVANCE and, therefore, the Liberal Party." The senator names Australian Digital Holdings, chaired by Maurice Newman, co-founder of ADVANCE, which the senator describes as "the Liberal aligned and Liberal funded—through the McCormack foundation—astroturfing group" that campaigned against the Indigenous Voice to Parliament. The senator also links ADVANCE to the Atlas Network and claims it is "aligned with the Liberal Party directly and are funded by the Liberal Party."

A separate passage from the Commonwealth Parliament, delivered by a member who says they have "experienced this environment from different sides—as a journalist asking questions and now as a member of parliament," argues that democracy is stronger because of media scrutiny and independence. That member supports bills providing "a framework to support Australian journalism" in the "fractured information age," but does not tie this to the Liberal Party. The record is otherwise limited on direct statements about Liberal Party media ownership.

sections.question: What has parliament said about the Music Bill 2026?
sections.answer:
The Music Bill 2026 was debated in the New South Wales Parliament, with the Government's second reading speech delivered by the Hon. John Graham, Minister for Music and the Night-time Economy. He described it as "world-leading" and "world-first" legislation, explaining that it creates a new Music Act to support the contemporary music industry, repeals the Sound NSW legislation, establishes a venue accreditation scheme, standardises noise assessment methodology for major festival sites, and prohibits decisions based solely on musical genre. He framed it as adopting a model similar to the Whitlam Government's support for the screen industry in the 1970s, arguing that without intervention, Australian music stories "will be wiped out by the algorithm."

Ms Cate Faehrmann, speaking for The Greens, supported the bill's intent but called it "welcome, but incomplete." She criticised the Government for a "profound contradiction" between its vibrancy claims and police operations that entered queer venues during Pride Month, and for failing to protect the Divine Playhouse venue from eviction. She also argued the bill is too narrowly confined to "contemporary music," excluding classical, jazz and experimental practice, and that it lacks recognition of music education as the industry's foundation. She criticised the model as "much more top-down" than the Whitlam-era Australian Film Commission.

In reply, Minister Graham rejected claims the Government stood by over Divine Playhouse, saying it "stands ready to work with the operators to establish a new home." He acknowledged her points about music education and the Whitlam benchmark were "probably fair," and invited her to back up criticisms with amendments. He defended the definition of contemporary music, saying it covers "all sorts of music" including country, jazz and blues. The bill passed its second reading, and the committee stage considered The Greens amendments Nos 1 to 12 and Government amendments Nos 1 to 9.

sections.question: What has parliament said about the Sound NSW Advisory Board Bill 2024?
sections.answer:
The Sound NSW Advisory Board Bill 2024 was debated in the New South Wales Parliament, with the Government moving to legislate the board to advise the Minister on the contemporary music industry. Ms Julia Finn (Granville), speaking on behalf of Ms Jenny Aitchison, said the bill "presents new legislation for the Sound NSW Advisory Board to advise the Minister on the strategic direction and sustainability of the contemporary music industry in New South Wales." She noted the bill would formalise the existing non-statutory board and "delivers on a commitment outlined in the Government's Creative Communities policy." The Government supported an Opposition amendment to require at least two board members be artists, with a specific definition of "artist," and supported two Greens amendments to include a member of the Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance and to introduce a review process.

Ms Cate Faehrmann (The Greens) said her party supported the bill but flagged amendments to improve diversity and representation, including increasing First Nations representation and ensuring at least one board member is a current MEAA member. The Hon. Jacqui Munro (Opposition) outlined the Opposition's amendments, arguing for at least two artists on the board and a clearer definition of "artist" to ensure "respected and experienced voices are in the room." The Hon. John Graham (Minister for Music and the Night-time Economy) said the Government wanted to formalise the board "to make sure that it is there for the long term," and acknowledged the challenge of keeping the board small enough to function while being diverse. The Hon. Mark Latham criticised the bill as an example of "industry policy and centralised planning," arguing the Government was "picking winners" with its $103 million investment in music. The bill passed its second reading, and amendments were dealt with in Committee.

sections.question: What have MPs said about media ownership concentration in Australia since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Several MPs have raised concerns about Australia's highly concentrated media market. One speaker noted that "Australia already has one of the most concentrated media markets in the developed world" and warned against any new funding mechanism that could "inadvertently makes the concentration worse." They cited organisations including the Local & Independent News Association, the Community Broadcasting Association of Australia, and the Public Interest Journalism Initiative as warning that the News Bargaining Incentive scheme could "entrench existing media concentration." Another MP said "The big players—News Corp, Nine, Seven West—dominate not just our television screens but the written word, the press and our radio waves," and argued that Australia needs "better and more important ways to support new players and media diversity." A further speaker expressed concern that the relevant bills "risk making Australia's media concentration worse rather than better" for small, independent, regional, multicultural and First Nations news organisations.

The record also includes a broader statement that "A healthy democracy requires... a plurality of voices, not a concentration of information in the hands of a few powerful global actors," and that it requires local, regional and community journalism. In a committee estimates hearing, a questioner asked about recent media mergers and acquisitions—specifically the proposed Paramount-owned Ten Network acquisition of WIN assets and the proposed DAZN acquisition of Foxtel—and what they mean for media diversity in Australia. Separately, a questioner asked whether the department was aware of Public Interest Journalism Initiative research indicating that, in the two decades leading up to 2024, the Australian news media landscape had shrunk by 19 per cent due to foreign social media companies.

sections.question: What was said about the news media bargaining code and tech platforms since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Several speakers addressed the news media bargaining code and tech platforms since July 2024. A government speaker said the code "didn't work" because tech companies could "simply opt out of the code by removing news content from their platforms," noting Meta did this briefly in 2021 and that in April 2024 Meta announced it would not renew commercial deals with Australian news media companies—deals "worth an estimated $70 million a year"—and removed the news tab from Facebook. The speaker argued platforms "can still reduce or withdraw their support for Australian journalism simply by changing how they choose to distribute and present news."

Coalition speakers criticised the government's response. One said Meta "walked away from the news media bargaining code" in April 2024, "abandoned its obligations, in breach of the law" and "threatened to take news off its digital platforms." Another claimed the coalition's 2021 code delivered "more than 30 commercial agreements, worth an estimated $250 million annually, to Australian news businesses," but that "the problem was never that the code failed. The problem was that the government failed to use it and failed to monitor it." A further coalition speaker said that when Meta walked away, "Labor chose to dismantle the framework rather than amending the existing code for changing circumstances," and that the government "spent the better part of two years dismantling the code and building a new one."

Government speakers defended the new approach. One said the package "strengthens the existing code by addressing that gap" where "a platform could remove news from its service and avoid the bargaining obligation." Another said the News Bargaining Incentive "is not intended to raise revenue" but "to encourage commercial deals between digital platforms and news publishers." A speaker from the crossbench opposed the bill, saying that under the 2021 code "the money went to the three or four biggest incumbents already dominating the market" and that the political establishment "hates" independent platforms and podcasters.

sections.question: What has parliament said about SBS headquarters?
sections.answer:
Several Victorian state parliamentarians debated a motion calling on the Allan Labor government to advocate for a Melbourne-based SBS headquarters. The motion's mover, Mr Mulholland (Liberals), noted that "of the 1319 SBS staff, 80 per cent were based in New South Wales, while only 14 per cent were based in Victoria" and expressed concern that a feasibility study indicated possible relocation of SBS headquarters from Artarmon to Western Sydney. He claimed that a senior SBS official told a 12 March 2025 committee hearing that the decision to base a new production hub in western Sydney "was one forced on SBS by the Albanese Labor government," despite the Minister for Communications claiming it was an SBS board initiative. The motion called on the Allan government to advocate for a Melbourne-based SBS headquarters in a multicultural location like Broadmeadows or Dandenong.

A Greens member supported the goal of a Melbourne-based SBS hub, saying "having a production hub... in a multicultural part of Melbourne means local jobs and means local stories." A Labor member opposed the motion, arguing it was "not about making a substantial difference to multicultural communities" but "just about making a statement," and noted the Allan government's investments in Melbourne's west. In the Commonwealth parliament, Mr Tim James (Willoughby) acknowledged "Special Broadcasting Service on its 50 years of service and its proud home in Artarmon," thanking SBS and wishing it "continued success in Artarmon." At a Commonwealth estimates hearing on 25 February 2025, a senator asked whether "a promise from the previous government that it would look at relocating SBS's headquarters... has come down to a proposal to do a business case on building a production hub in Western Sydney."

eras.question: How did parliament argue about media ownership between 1993 and 2009? The debates of the period included Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Digital Television Switch-over) Bill 2008, Auditor-General’s Reports and Australian Broadcasting Corporation Amendment Bill 2006.
eras.answer:
The parliamentary record shows sustained argument over media ownership reform, with the central divide being whether to relax or retain cross-media and foreign ownership restrictions. A Labor speaker attacked the Howard government for initially scrapping a promised full public inquiry into cross-media rules and instead holding a "private, in camera departmental review", which unsurprisingly recommended watering down or abolishing those rules. That speaker also claimed the government’s digital television legislation was being "rammed through the parliament" and left the minister with "enormous powers", while noting that government backbenchers had spoken out against the Prime Minister’s plans before he was "rolled" on the issue. In 2006, Labor senators rejected the government’s media ownership bill package, with one Labor senator saying the bills reflected "the most significant changes to Australia's media laws since the introduction of the cross-media ownership laws back in 1987" and that the government had treated the committee process "with contempt". The Australian Democrats also opposed the 2006 changes, arguing cross-media laws should not be altered until competition improved, Telstra was divested from Foxtel and the HFC cable, full digitisation was achieved, and new services were more mature.

Government speakers defended the reforms as necessary modernisation. One coalition speaker said the 2006 bills would "bring Australian media law into the 21st century" and discard "extremely outmoded" models, noting the laws were crafted nearly 20 years earlier in a world without widespread internet, pay TV, or digital radio. Another government speaker, supporting the 2002 media ownership bill, argued the reforms would provide consumers with greater media diversity and help strengthen the industry, citing the Productivity Commission’s 2000 finding that there was "no reason why foreign ownership in the media should not be regulated in the same way as other industries". That speaker also stressed that protections remained, including the Foreign Acquisitions and Takeovers Act 1975, the Trade Practices Act, and requirements for editorial separation and minimum local news. A further coalition speaker in 2006 claimed the package was the product of "extensive consultation" since 2005 and balanced industry, consumer and stakeholder views. The record also shows debate over the 2008 digital switch-over bill, with The Australian Greens supporting clear criteria for assessing regional readiness to make the minister’s decision transparent.

eras.question: How did parliament argue about media ownership between 2010 and 2019? The debates of the period included Suspension of Standing and Sessional Orders: Order of Business and Library Amendment Bill 2019.
eras.answer:
The record shows that media ownership was raised in the context of a suspension of standing orders debate, with a minister rejecting an opposition question’s premise. The minister said: “I reject the underpinning assertion on which that question is based. It is an attempt to misrepresent what the Prime Minister said. It is a total misrepresentation—and then you add the bile and you add all the rest on top and you come up with that question.” He then claimed that those on the other side “want to see a further contraction in media ownership in this country” and “would prefer to see fewer media owners than exist today.” An opposition senator interjected on relevance, saying the minister was “rambling about the ownership of media in Australia rather than dealing with the question which was specifically about the timing for the passage of legislation.”

In a separate passage, a speaker noted the debate was occurring “in the context of media ownership, with moves by Mr Packer to take up a greater shareholding in Channel 10,” and argued: “We need to revisit the debate about the power of the concentration of media ownership in this country. This bill touches on that to a degree.” Another passage mentioned a government-announced independent media inquiry into print media regulation, including online publications and the Press Council, to be conducted by former Federal Court judge Ray Finkelstein QC. A point of order was then raised asking whether the inquiry’s terms of reference permitted it to look at “the concentration of newspaper ownership.” The record is limited to these fragments; no passage names the parliament in which these exchanges occurred, and none addresses the Library Amendment Bill 2019.

eras.question: How did parliament argue about media ownership between 2020 and the middle of 2024? The debates of the period included Defamation (Miscellaneous) Amendment Bill, Regional Media and Regional media.
eras.answer:
The debates show deep concern about media concentration and the decline of regional media, with Labor and crossbench members repeatedly criticising the government's record. In the Commonwealth Parliament, a Labor speaker noted that "Australia has one of the most concentrated media markets in the world" and that the government's 2017 media law changes "repealed the two-out-of-three cross-media control rule, which permitted Australia's already highly concentrated media sector to become even more concentrated." The same speaker said that since those changes, "around 200 newspapers have closed and hundreds of journalism jobs have been lost," with "around 21 local government areas without coverage from a single local newspaper." Labor also claimed the government's changes were heralded as "a new era for Australia's media" but that the reality was different, and that the government had failed to implement genuine holistic reform.

On regional media specifically, multiple speakers in the Commonwealth Parliament described a crisis. A Labor speaker said regional media had been "hit by a triple whammy: digital disruption, COVID-19 and, of course, this government," and cited ACCC data that "between 2008 and 2018, 106 local and regional newspaper titles closed across Australia, a net 15 per cent decrease." Another Labor speaker said the government had "failed regional media by failing to reform the legislative framework and failing to deliver effective direct and indirect support to industry in a timely manner," and that the Broadcasting Services Amendment (Regional Commercial Radio and Other Measures) Bill 2020 was "late, it's inadequate and it sells regional Australia short." A Centre Alliance speaker said small regional publishers received only "around 15 per cent of the funding" from the Public Interest News Gathering program, with bigger media companies receiving the bulk. In the Victorian Parliament, an independent member moved a reasoned amendment against removing the requirement for government notices to be published in print newspapers, warning it would hurt regional newspapers' viability and community access to information, while a Liberal member supported amendments to ensure notices "must be published in a print newspaper circulating in those parts of regional or suburban Victoria."

key_moments.brief: The Evidence Amendment (Journalists' Privilege) Bill 2010 introduces a rebuttable presumption that journalists cannot be compelled to reveal confidential sources, a reform prompted by the 2007 conviction of Herald Sun journalists Michael Harvey and Gerard McManus for refusing to identify a source. The bill, which received cross-party support, was referred to the Senate Legal and Constitutional Affairs Legislation Committee for inquiry and report by 23 November 2010.

key_moments.title: Public Broadcasting
key_moments.speaker: Shaoquett Moselmane
key_moments.brief: The speaker opposed any sale or privatisation of the ABC and SBS, praising their role in providing diverse, quality reporting and opportunities for young journalists, and criticised the Turnbull government for allegedly seeking to restrict the broadcasters.

key_moments.title: Regional media
key_moments.speaker: Sheed
key_moments.brief: The speaker argued that regional media in Australia is in crisis due to closures, consolidations, and job losses, citing the loss of 138 newsrooms according to the Public Interest Journalism Initiative, and called for government support including advertising in local newspapers, a revamp of the Broadcasting Services Act, and lower thresholds for public interest journalism grants to preserve democratic accountability.

key_moments.title: News Media Bargaining Code
key_moments.speaker: Michelle Rowland
key_moments.brief: The speaker supported the mandatory bargaining code bill but criticised the government for delays and failing to implement broader ACCC recommendations, noting that around 200 newspapers have closed and hundreds of journalism jobs lost since 2017 media law changes.

key_moments.title: Freedom of speech
key_moments.speaker: David Davis
key_moments.brief: The speaker argued that the Communications Legislation Amendment (Combatting Misinformation and Disinformation) Bill 2024 threatens freedom of speech in Victoria by giving overly broad powers to digital platforms such as Facebook, YouTube, and TikTok, and called on the Premier to intervene with the federal government to stop the bill.

lede.text: The debate over media ownership in Australian parliaments has shifted from whether to relax cross-media and foreign ownership rules in the 2000s to how to counter concentration and sustain journalism in the platform age. Labor and crossbench members now argue that Australia's highly concentrated market, deepened by the 2017 repeal of the two-out-of-three rule and the withdrawal of Meta from the bargaining code, needs new support for smaller and regional outlets. The coalition defends its 2021 news media bargaining code as having delivered hundreds of millions to news businesses and blames Labor for dismantling it rather than amending it when Meta walked away. The current fight centres on the Labor government's News Bargaining Incentive and News Journalism Payments Bill 2026, with government speakers insisting the charge is an incentive for commercial deals, not a revenue raiser.
